segs.text: Section thirty seven. Herbal, food and nondrug interactions. Herbs, foods, cigarette smoke and ethanol act as precipitants through the same mechanisms as drugs. An herbal product may be one herb or several, and one herb may contain many compounds with many activities. Some contain prescription medications, some contaminants such as metals or other toxic plants. They are not regulated, and potency varies batch to batch with harvest stage, drying time, extraction solvents, and shelf life and storage. So herbs interact at the same transport, metabolism and receptor sites as drugs.

St. John's wort, used for depression, shows how many mechanisms one herb can have. It induces sip three A four, lowering protease inhibitors, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, cyclosporin and digoxin. It induces two C nine and one A two, lowering warfarin. It increases intestinal P glycoprotein efflux, lowering digoxin, calcium channel blockers and simvastatin, so it does not raise digoxin. And it adds serotonin activity with S S R Is, triptans and monoamine oxidase inhibitors, risking serotonin toxicity.

Narrow therapeutic index drugs are at greater risk, and warfarin is the classic example. Vitamin K is warfarin's antidote. Coenzyme Q ten has a structure similar to vitamin K, and wheat grass contains high levels of vitamin K, so both may cause inadequate anticoagulation. Spinach and broccoli contain vitamin K, which pharmacodynamically antagonizes warfarin. Ginger, garlic and feverfew work another way: they directly inhibit platelets, a different mechanism from warfarin, so bleeding risk increases.

Food can increase, decrease, or not affect absorption, and foods that change stomach p H may change bioavailability. A common interaction is a drug complexing with food in the gut, such as quinolone antibiotics with calcium, which reduces absorption; that is complexation, not an enzyme effect. Food can also compete for metabolizing enzymes, making it an inhibitor, or induce them, giving toxic or subtherapeutic levels. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors block the breakdown of catecholamines; tyramine from red wine and cheese uses the same enzyme, so it builds up and may cause a hypertensive crisis.

Smoking and ethanol are the most common chemical drug interactions. Smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that induce sip one A two, lowering theophylline, diazepam and tricyclic antidepressants; theophylline in asthmatics must not go subtherapeutic.

Ethanol can increase or decrease hepatic enzyme activity. Its sip one A two induction lowers clozapine, cyclobenzaprine, imipramine and naproxen. Its induction of two E one and three A increases the possibility of acetaminophen liver damage, hepatotoxicity. So the acetaminophen risk comes from two E one and three A, not one A two.
